dictionary; when the two disagree, obey the specification.

## What this applies to

Apply STE to prose: explanations, reports, recommendations, questions, and
summaries.

Do **not** apply STE to these. Give them unchanged:

- Code, in a block or inline.
- File paths, identifiers, commands, flags, and branch names.
- Quoted output: errors, logs, test results, diffs, tool results.
- Text that a standard controls: commit messages (Conventional Commits), PR
  titles, and the code comments of a repository.

Do not repair the grammar of quoted material. Quote it exactly.

## Words

1. Use a word from the approved dictionary, a technical name, or a technical
   verb. Use no other word.
2. One word has one meaning. One meaning has one word. Do not use two words for
   one thing in the same reply.
3. Use a word in one part of speech only. `check` is a verb; for the noun, write
   `the check`  only if the tool is named that.
4. Do not use contractions. Write `do not`, not `don't`.
5. Do not use a word that shows feeling about the work: `unfortunately`,
   `obviously`, `simply`, `just`, `clearly`, `of course`, `nicely`, `elegant`.
6. Do not use an idiom or a metaphor. Write what occurs.

### Technical names

A technical name is a noun that names a thing in the domain. Technical names are
approved. Use them.

For software work, these are technical names: `commit`, `branch`, `merge`,
`rebase`, `repository`, `function`, `type`, `test`, `gate`, `worktree`. Use the
name that the repository uses. If the repository has a vocabulary document (for
example `CONTEXT.md`), that document is the list of approved technical names.
Use those terms exactly.

### Technical verbs

If no approved verb names the action, use the verb of the domain: `commit`,
`merge`, `rebase`, `push`, `compile`, `deploy`. Use one such verb for one
action, always the same one.

### Approved words for common unapproved ones

| Write         | Do not write                                            |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| about         | approximately, regarding, concerning, with respect to    |
| after         | subsequent to, following                                 |
| also          | in addition, furthermore, moreover                       |
| because       | due to the fact that, owing to, since (for a cause)      |
| before        | prior to, in advance of                                  |
| but           | however, nevertheless, nonetheless                       |
| can           | is able to, is capable of                                |
| change        | modify, alter, amend, revise                             |
| check         | verify, validate, confirm                                |

| enough        | sufficient, adequate                                     |
| find          | locate, ascertain, determine                             |
| get           | obtain, acquire                                          |
| give, supply  | provide, furnish                                         |
| help          | assist, aid, facilitate                                  |
| if            | in the event that, in case                               |
| keep          | retain, preserve, maintain                               |
| let           | allow, permit, enable                                    |
| make sure     | ensure                                                   |
| many          | numerous, a large number of                              |
| more          | additional, further                                      |
| must          | shall, is required to                                    |
| must not      | shall not, is prohibited from                            |
| need          | require, necessitate                                     |
| now           | at this time, currently, presently                       |
| only          | solely, exclusively, merely                              |
| part          | component, element, portion                              |
| problem       | issue, concern                                           |
| put           | place, position (as a verb)                              |
| same          | identical, equivalent                                    |
| see           | refer to, consult                                        |
| show          | indicate, demonstrate, illustrate, display (as a verb)   |
| so            | thus, therefore, hence, consequently                     |
| start         | commence, initiate, begin                                |
| stop          | cease, terminate, discontinue, halt                      |
| tell          | inform, notify, advise                                   |
| then          | subsequently, thereafter                                 |
| try to        | attempt to, endeavor to                                  |
| use           | utilize, employ, leverage                                |
| with          | by means of, via                                         |

## Verbs

7. Use the active voice. Write `I ran the tests`, not `the tests were run`.
8. Use these verb forms only: the infinitive, the imperative, the simple
   present, the simple past, the simple future.
9. Do not use a perfect tense. Write `I pushed the branch`, not `I have pushed
   the branch`.
10. Do not use a progressive tense and do not use an `-ing` word. Write `I run
    the gates now`, not `I am running the gates`.
11. A past participle can be an adjective: `the failed test` is correct. A
    present participle cannot: write `the test that fails`, not `the failing
    test`.
12. Do not turn a verb into a noun. Write `I rebased the branch`, not `I did a
    rebase of the branch`.

## Sentences

13. A sentence in a procedure has 20 words or fewer.
14. A sentence in descriptive text has 25 words or fewer.
15. A paragraph in descriptive text has 6 sentences or fewer.
16. One sentence gives one idea. Split a long sentence. Do not join two ideas
    with a semicolon or a dash.
17. Keep the articles `a`, `an`, and `the`. Keep `that` and `which`. Do not
    remove words to make the text shorter.
18. A noun cluster has 3 words or fewer. Write `the cache of the kernel data`,
    not `the kernel data cache repaint key`.
19. Put the words in the usual order: subject, verb, object.

20. Give one instruction in one sentence.
21. Start an instruction with the verb: `Run the gates.` `Rebase the branch.`
22. Put more than two conditions or steps in a vertical list.
23. Give the steps in the order of the work.

## Descriptive text

24. Say what is true. Do not say what is not there and do not say what did not
    occur, unless the user asked.
25. Give the cause before the effect.
26. Use the same term for one thing in the whole reply.

## Warnings and cautions

27. Put a warning before the step it applies to, not after.
28. Start a warning with a command or with the condition. Write `Do not push to
    main.` or `If the gate fails, stop.`
29. Give the risk in one sentence.

Not STE:

> only touches three files, none of which overlap anything that's landed, so
> there weren't any conflicts to worry about. Currently running the gates.

STE:

> I rebased #1119 onto main. The branch changes 3 files. No file is also changed
> by a merged branch, so the rebase had no conflict. I run the gates now.

Not STE:

> Unfortunately the failing test was caused by a stale projection, which is why
> simply bumping the timeout wouldn't have helped here.

STE:

> A stale projection caused the test to fail. A longer timeout does not correct
> a stale projection.

The approved dictionary has about 900 words. The table above gives only the
words that occur most in this work. If you are not sure that a word is approved,
use a shorter and more common word.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

## linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for .pen design files (web/mobile apps and websites). Use it to read, generate, and validate designs.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via "pencil" MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Always call get_app_state({ include_schema: true, include_canvas_design: true, include_scripts_and_shaders: false }) if you don't have the current .pen file schema in the context. All three flags are required. Knowing the schema is required to use any other Pencil MCP tool.

Tools: get_app_state, get_guidelines, execute, get_screenshot, export_nodes, export_html.
Also: browser.

## plugin:vercel:vercel
Use the available Vercel tools and their input schemas. Discover the intended team and project before choosing resource IDs.

Reuse team, project, and deployment IDs supplied by the user or returned by tools. When scope is unknown, discover teams, then projects in the selected team. Ask only if the intended target remains ambiguous. Respect a project-scoped connection; do not guess combinations of IDs.

For troubleshooting, inspect the relevant deployment state, build output, or runtime logs before changing configuration. Use documentation search when platform behavior is unclear.

Filter reads to the relevant project, time range, and fields supported by the operation. Follow pagination when a complete list is needed; state when results are partial or truncated. Batch independent calls; wait for results before making dependent calls.

Inspect the target before modifying an existing resource when a read is available, and verify the resulting state afterward. For purchases, follow get_purchase_quote and the dedicated confirmation tool. Never decrypt environment values unless explicitly requested.

Inspect each call result, including failures within a batch. Correct invalid inputs from the returned schema. For access or not-found errors, verify scope instead of repeating guessed IDs; do not assume every not-found error means no access. Retry transient failures only when safe, and check state before retrying a write with an uncertain outcome. Distinguish accepted or pending work from completed work.

For all Typescript projects, prefer the use of string literals over typescript enums

When doing a task spin up sub-agents and try to retain your context as an orchestrator, giving small jobs (that will fit entirely in context) to sub-agents.

## Continuous Learning Protocol

When completing a significant piece of work (migrations, new features, complex debugging, architectural changes):

1. **Identify learnings** - What would have made this task easier if known upfront?
2. **Document in `~/.claude/learnings/LEARNINGS.md`** - Add dated entries with:
   - Problem encountered
   - Lesson learned
   - Concrete action for future tasks
3. **Review learnings** at the start of similar tasks to avoid repeating mistakes

Key categories to capture:
- Schema/database gotchas for this codebase
- Performance patterns (row-by-row vs set-based operations)
- Testing patterns and common failure modes
- Tool/command usage that wasn't obvious

## SSH Connections

Always authenticate SSH/SCP via the 1Password SSH agent — never write private keys from 1Password to disk for `ssh -i`/`scp -i` (it leaks key material to disk and to logs/transcripts).

- The agent socket on macOS is `~/Library/Group Containers/2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password/t/agent.sock`. Export `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` to point at it (or rely on a global `IdentityAgent` in `~/.ssh/config`), then connect with plain `ssh user@host` — 1Password serves the key and prompts for biometric approval.
- Confirm the right key is loaded with `SSH_AUTH_SOCK=<sock> ssh-add -l` before connecting.
- Only fall back to a temp key file if the agent is genuinely unavailable, and securely delete it immediately afterward.

## Developer Profile

> Generated by GSD from session_analysis. Run `/gsd-profile-user --refresh` to update.

| Dimension | Rating | Confidence |
|-----------|--------|------------|
| Communication | terse-direct | HIGH |
| Decisions | fast-intuitive | MEDIUM |
| Explanations | concise | LOW |
| Debugging | diagnostic | MEDIUM |
| UX Philosophy | pragmatic | LOW |
| Vendor Choices | pragmatic-fast | LOW |
| Frustrations | instruction-adherence | LOW |
| Learning | self-directed | LOW |

**Directives:**
- **Communication:** Keep responses brief and action-oriented. Match this developer's terse, imperative style. Do not pad with preamble; execute the stated request directly.
- **Decisions:** Present a clear recommended action rather than a menu of options. This developer decides fast; offer one strong path forward and proceed once confirmed.
- **Explanations:** Give brief, decision-focused answers with the key reasoning, not exhaustive walkthroughs. Try concise depth and ask if they want more detail when the topic is complex.
- **Debugging:** When debugging, identify and explain the root cause alongside the fix. Acknowledge the developer's own diagnostic observations and confirm or refute their reasoning rather than just applying a patch.
- **UX Philosophy:** Ensure UI changes are functional and not visibly broken, but do not over-invest in design polish unless asked. Try a pragmatic balance and ask about visual priorities when working on frontend.
- **Vendor Choices:** Recommend practical, working tooling choices weighted toward cost and speed of delivery. Try suggesting a sensible default and confirm if they want to evaluate alternatives.
- **Frustrations:** Follow established workflow instructions and persisted memories precisely; do not repeat past mistakes. Scope changes tightly to what was requested and avoid touching files that do not need to change.
- **Learning:** Answer specific, scoped questions directly and respect that this developer reasons about the code independently. Avoid unsolicited tutorials or example dumps; provide depth only when asked.

## Project Context

CipherBox is a privacy-first, zero-knowledge E2EE personal cloud storage system on IPFS/IPNS. The repo is mid-rewrite: **v2 is being built on `main`** against the blueprint corpus below; v1 is frozen on branch `v1` (tag `v1-freeze`) and receives no changes.

## Terminology Standards

Use the v2 ubiquitous language defined in `CONTEXT.md` — every domain term (scope, epoch, ascent link, grant blob, adoption gate, floor law, eager set, …) has exactly one name there. General conventions: `publicKey`/`privateKey`/`ipnsName`/`ipnsRecord` spelled out in full camelCase for API fields, snake_case for database columns.

## Critical Security Rules

1. **Never** store `privateKey` or any seed in localStorage/sessionStorage
2. **Never** log sensitive keys or seeds
3. **Never** send unencrypted keys to the server — the server is zero-knowledge and NEVER sees plaintext or unencrypted keys
4. **All crypto lives in `crates/core`** — TypeScript has no codec or crypto of its own; never implement crypto in TS. **One exception: browser-held key custody via WebCrypto**, for a key that must be non-extractable, or must exist before the engine has a session. The engine cannot serve either case — a WASM implementation necessarily materializes key bytes in linear memory, which is the property non-extractability exists to deny, and before `start(secret)` there is no session to derive from. Conditions, all of them: the key protects local state only, it derives nothing in the KDF catalog, it touches no wire format and no KAT, and it never leaves WebCrypto. Two live instances — the Core Kit store's wrapping key (`apps/web/src/auth/sealedStore.ts`), and the device identity key that signs a device-approval exchange before reconstruction ([ADR 0009](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0009-device-approval-is-a-bound-rendezvous.md)). Anything protocol-shaped is still Rust, without exception.
5. Primitives are fixed by `blueprint/core.md`: XChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing, BLAKE3 tree KDF, X25519 + HPKE key wrapping, REDACTED signing — no key derives outside the frozen KDF edge catalog
6. Every resolved record passes the adoption gate; a failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness
7. Clear sensitive material from memory after use (zeroize at the terminal owner only — a callee must not zero caller-owned buffers)
8. **Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry** — when a decode/verify path hard-rejects an invariant violation (a trust/malformed check), the matching encode/produce path MUST enforce the same invariant with a **release-active** check that returns `Err` — never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`, which are stripped in release. Otherwise a release build can sign and publish bytes its own decoder always rejects (an unopenable ledger/commitment/body). Keep these encode-side checks consistent with the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention, and cover them with a test that fires in a release build.

## API Contract and Clients

There are **no generated API clients** and no codegen loop. The engine contains the single hand-written Rust API client; the NestJS API's OpenAPI document is a committed docs artifact, not a build input. The contract is enforced by the live contract-test suite (the sdk-e2e descendant) running the real client against a real API instance on every PR — see `blueprint/testing.md`.

## Code Generation Guidelines

1. All engine, codec, and crypto logic is Rust (`crates/core`, `crates/engine`); TypeScript exists only in `packages/client` (WASM wrapper, browser seams), `packages/login` (host-agnostic login sequencing), `packages/auth-ui` (the React auth surfaces both hosts render), `apps/web` (React UI), `apps/desktop` (the Tauri shell chrome) and `tests/*` (the e2e harnesses)
2. Use `Uint8Array`/`Vec<u8>` for binary data, not strings
3. Determinism is injected: entropy, time, and policy enter as parameters/seam traits — never call clocks or RNGs directly in core/engine logic
4. Every suite must block a merge in a named CI gate the day it lands (`blueprint/testing.md` law 1); assert behavior, never source text

## Code Style

### Comments

Comments explain _why_, not _what_, and stay short. **If you need a paragraph-long comment to justify why a workaround is OK, the code is wrong — fix the code.** A long apologia for a hack is a smell: rework the code so it no longer needs defending, rather than documenting the shortcut. Reserve multi-line comments for genuinely non-obvious domain rationale — a spec citation, a cryptographic invariant, a wire-format or fail-closed constraint — not for excusing a shortcut.

Three recurring shapes of this smell go beyond excusing a hack — avoid all three:

- **Absence-justifying comments** — prose explaining why a path that is _not_ in the code does not happen (e.g. "`replay()` does not run here, so `decode_queue` is the only source at this stage"). It bloats the diff and rots into a falsehood the moment that path is wired — a stale in-code claim that actively misleads. Describe what the present code does; a bare cross-reference suffices if a reader must know a related path lives elsewhere.
- **Unchanged-code apologia** — a doc block defending code this change does not modify (e.g. why a parameter stays a raw borrow, on a function the diff leaves untouched). It is scope creep into untouched code and reads as pre-emptive defensiveness. Leave that rationale where it already lives.
- **Tracker references** — a bare `#1234` claims something about the _tracker_, not the code, so nothing in CI, review, or the type system catches it drifting when the issue closes, splits, or gets re-scoped. State the condition instead: `the real wiring is #1026` becomes `the real wiring is not landed`, which is checkable from the code and stops being true in the same diff that falsifies it. Enforced by `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` (the **Tracker Refs** gate). Exempt: citations of the frozen decision corpus, whether written `FSM1/cipher-box-next#32` or bare as `#33 D6` — this repo's issue numbers share an ever-increasing counter with its PRs and passed 1000 long ago, so a one- or two-digit `#NN` can only be cipher-box-next. Commit messages and PR bodies are also exempt: they are timestamped and do not rot.

State genuine non-obvious domain rationale **once**, at its home (the type or definition), not restated on every caller. These cost real review cycles — `/simplify`, CodeRabbit, and Greptile all flag them.

Length discipline for the permitted domain-rationale exception: state each invariant **once** and prefer a one-line cross-reference to the blueprint / `CONTEXT.md` over re-deriving it in prose. Do not narrate the happy path — the code is the narrative, and a comment restating what the next lines plainly do rots out of sync and misleads. A module header past ~25 lines is almost always restating the spec: keep only the rationale that is non-obvious _from the code itself_ and cite the blueprint for the rest.

## Architecture Pillars

- **Auth:** Web3Auth key derivation; challenge-signature login; short-lived JWT + rotating refresh
- **Storage:** IPFS content, IPNS metadata — the network is canonical; clients verify records cryptographically; CipherBox infra (Kubo, someguy) is accelerator-only and the API never serves records
- **Keys:** seeded per-scope derivation with key-regression epochs; rotation = O(1) root cut + lazy wave (`CONTEXT.md`)
- **One Rust core:** desktop links it natively, web loads it as WASM in a worker; one implementation, one KAT set
- **Sync:** pull-only focus-window polling, cache-first, offline op queue; no push in v2.0 (seam ready)
- **Desktop:** Tauri + FUSE mount (FUSE-T SMB on macOS, libfuse3 on Linux, WinFsp on Windows)
- **No TEE:** the republisher is a keyless re-PUT module inside the API; client-signed 90-day EOLs

## Out of Scope

- Billing/payments, mobile apps, real-time collaborative editing, team accounts
- Vault import (cut in v2), client-side search (deferred, designed-for)
- Executing anything against the frozen `v1` branch

## Git Workflow

### Branch Protection Rules

- **NEVER push directly to `main` branch** - all changes must go through feature branches and PRs
- Create feature branches with descriptive names (e.g., `feat/add-auth`, `fix/ipns-publish`)
- All commits should be made on feature branches first
- Merge to main only via pull requests

### Branch Naming

- `feat/` - New features
- `fix/` - Bug fixes
- `docs/` - Documentation updates
- `refactor/` - Code refactoring
- `chore/` - Maintenance tasks

### Commit Messages

Commits must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format:

```text
type(optional-scope): description

[optional body]
```

Valid types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Any scope string is allowed (e.g., `feat(api): add health endpoint`). A custom commitlint rule additionally rejects parenthesized text in the subject line (it breaks Release Please parsing).

Enforcement: commitlint is configured via `commitlint.config.js`, and PR titles are validated in CI by `.github/workflows/pr-title.yml`. Note that the husky `commit-msg` hook was replaced by an Entire CLI wrapper and currently does not run commitlint locally — follow the format regardless, since CI will reject non-conforming PR titles.

### No Tool Attribution

A commit message, a PR title, a PR body, an issue, and a review comment carry **no attribution to the tool that wrote them** — no `🤖 Generated with …` line, no `Co-Authored-By:` trailer naming an assistant, no session link. This holds however the text was produced.

The authorship that matters is the commit author and the PR author, which git and GitHub already record. A generated-by line adds nothing a reader can act on and turns every PR body into an advertisement.

Agent harnesses commonly append such a line by default. That default does not apply here: strip it before opening or editing a PR, and check the rendered body afterwards rather than trusting that it was never added.

### Mandatory PR Review Flow

Every code PR runs these review gates after it is opened as a **draft**, before it is driven toward merge — mandatory, not optional:

1. `/simplify` — tighten the diff: remove speculative generality, dead abstraction, and duplication.
2. `/security-review` — trust boundaries, fail-closed behavior, auth/expiry gates, injection, DoS/resource exhaustion, concurrency, and determinism seams.
3. `/crypto-privacy-review` — **required whenever the diff touches crypto**: `crates/core` primitives, key/seal material, or trust-boundary and fail-closed reads.

Run each on the PR's own diff (`git diff main...HEAD`) and fold real findings back into the code and tests before requesting a CodeRabbit/Greptile review. If a slash-command skill is unavailable in your environment, do a rigorous manual pass against that review's checklist instead — never skip a gate. Self-review is the floor, not the ceiling: layer an independent reviewer pass on crypto- and trust-critical PRs. A pure documentation change with no code surface is exempt.

### Releases & Versioning

See the `releases` skill (`.claude/skills/releases/SKILL.md`) for the v2 release scheme, version surfaces, staging tag pipeline, and the v1 freeze. Normative source: `blueprint/deploy.md`.

# CipherBox - AI Agent Instructions

## Project Context

CipherBox is a privacy-first, zero-knowledge E2EE personal cloud storage system on IPFS/IPNS. The repo is mid-rewrite: **v2 is being built on `main`** against the blueprint corpus below; v1 is frozen on branch `v1` (tag `v1-freeze`) and receives no changes.

## Documentation Structure

The normative source of truth for the v2 build:

| Document                  | Purpose                                                       |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CONTEXT.md`              | The v2 ubiquitous language — use these terms, exactly         |
| `blueprint/core.md`       | `crates/core` — wire formats, crypto, KDF catalog, KAT regime |
| `blueprint/engine.md`     | `crates/engine` — the one stateful brain, seam traits, gates  |
| `blueprint/api.md`        | API residual surface, registry, mailbox, republisher          |
| `blueprint/web-client.md` | WASM hosting, tab leadership, `packages/client`, `apps/web`   |
| `blueprint/desktop.md`    | FS projection, host adapters, Tauri shell                     |
| `blueprint/testing.md`    | Suite map, CI gates, coverage policy                          |
| `blueprint/deploy.md`     | Freeze mechanics, release management, staging pipeline        |

The as-built v1 spec corpus, ADRs, and all design-decision history live in [FSM1/cipher-box-next](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next) (wayfinder map issue 1 indexes every decision). The `docs/` folder is v1 legacy — being rewritten during the build; trust `blueprint/` when they conflict.

## Terminology Standards

Use the v2 ubiquitous language defined in `CONTEXT.md` — every domain term (scope, epoch, ascent link, grant blob, adoption gate, floor law, eager set, …) has exactly one name there. General conventions: `publicKey`/`privateKey`/`ipnsName`/`ipnsRecord` spelled out in full camelCase for API fields, snake_case for database columns.

## Critical Security Rules

1. **Never** store `privateKey` or any seed in localStorage/sessionStorage
2. **Never** log sensitive keys or seeds
3. **Never** send unencrypted keys to the server — the server is zero-knowledge and NEVER sees plaintext or unencrypted keys
4. **All crypto lives in `crates/core`** — TypeScript has no codec or crypto of its own; never implement crypto in TS. **One exception: browser-held key custody via WebCrypto**, for a key that must be non-extractable, or must exist before the engine has a session. The engine cannot serve either case — a WASM implementation necessarily materializes key bytes in linear memory, which is the property non-extractability exists to deny, and before `start(secret)` there is no session to derive from. Conditions, all of them: the key protects local state only, it derives nothing in the KDF catalog, it touches no wire format and no KAT, and it never leaves WebCrypto. Two live instances — the Core Kit store's wrapping key (`apps/web/src/auth/sealedStore.ts`), and the device identity key that signs a device-approval exchange before reconstruction ([ADR 0009](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0009-device-approval-is-a-bound-rendezvous.md)). Anything protocol-shaped is still Rust, without exception.
5. Primitives are fixed by `blueprint/core.md`: XChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing, BLAKE3 tree KDF, X25519 + HPKE key wrapping, REDACTED signing — no key derives outside the frozen KDF edge catalog
6. Every resolved record passes the adoption gate; a failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness
7. Clear sensitive material from memory after use (zeroize at the terminal owner only — a callee must not zero caller-owned buffers)
8. **Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry** — when a decode/verify path hard-rejects an invariant violation (a trust/malformed check), the matching encode/produce path MUST enforce the same invariant with a **release-active** check that returns `Err` — never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`, which are stripped in release. Otherwise a release build can sign and publish bytes its own decoder always rejects (an unopenable ledger/commitment/body). Keep these encode-side checks consistent with the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention, and cover them with a test that fires in a release build.

## API Contract and Clients

There are **no generated API clients** and no codegen loop. The engine contains the single hand-written Rust API client; the NestJS API's OpenAPI document is a committed docs artifact, not a build input. The contract is enforced by the live contract-test suite (the sdk-e2e descendant) running the real client against a real API instance on every PR — see `blueprint/testing.md`.

## Code Generation Guidelines

1. All engine, codec, and crypto logic is Rust (`crates/core`, `crates/engine`); TypeScript exists only in `packages/client` (WASM wrapper, browser seams), `packages/login` (host-agnostic login sequencing), `packages/auth-ui` (the React auth surfaces both hosts render), `apps/web` (React UI), `apps/desktop` (the Tauri shell chrome) and `tests/*` (the e2e harnesses)
2. Use `Uint8Array`/`Vec<u8>` for binary data, not strings
3. Determinism is injected: entropy, time, and policy enter as parameters/seam traits — never call clocks or RNGs directly in core/engine logic
4. Every suite must block a merge in a named CI gate the day it lands (`blueprint/testing.md` law 1); assert behavior, never source text

## Code Style

### Comments

Comments explain _why_, not _what_, and stay short. **If you need a paragraph-long comment to justify why a workaround is OK, the code is wrong — fix the code.** A long apologia for a hack is a smell: rework the code so it no longer needs defending, rather than documenting the shortcut. Reserve multi-line comments for genuinely non-obvious domain rationale — a spec citation, a cryptographic invariant, a wire-format or fail-closed constraint — not for excusing a shortcut.

Three recurring shapes of this smell go beyond excusing a hack — avoid all three:

- **Absence-justifying comments** — prose explaining why a path that is _not_ in the code does not happen (e.g. "`replay()` does not run here, so `decode_queue` is the only source at this stage"). It bloats the diff and rots into a falsehood the moment that path is wired — a stale in-code claim that actively misleads. Describe what the present code does; a bare cross-reference suffices if a reader must know a related path lives elsewhere.
- **Unchanged-code apologia** — a doc block defending code this change does not modify (e.g. why a parameter stays a raw borrow, on a function the diff leaves untouched). It is scope creep into untouched code and reads as pre-emptive defensiveness. Leave that rationale where it already lives.
- **Tracker references** — a bare `#1234` claims something about the _tracker_, not the code, so nothing in CI, review, or the type system catches it drifting when the issue closes, splits, or gets re-scoped. State the condition instead: `the real wiring is #1026` becomes `the real wiring is not landed`, which is checkable from the code and stops being true in the same diff that falsifies it. Enforced by `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` (the **Tracker Refs** gate). Exempt: citations of the frozen decision corpus, whether written `FSM1/cipher-box-next#32` or bare as `#33 D6` — this repo's issue numbers share an ever-increasing counter with its PRs and passed 1000 long ago, so a one- or two-digit `#NN` can only be cipher-box-next. Commit messages and PR bodies are also exempt: they are timestamped and do not rot.

State genuine non-obvious domain rationale **once**, at its home (the type or definition), not restated on every caller. These cost real review cycles — `/simplify`, CodeRabbit, and Greptile all flag them.

Length discipline for the permitted domain-rationale exception: state each invariant **once** and prefer a one-line cross-reference to the blueprint / `CONTEXT.md` over re-deriving it in prose. Do not narrate the happy path — the code is the narrative, and a comment restating what the next lines plainly do rots out of sync and misleads. A module header past ~25 lines is almost always restating the spec: keep only the rationale that is non-obvious _from the code itself_ and cite the blueprint for the rest.

## Architecture Pillars

- **Auth:** Web3Auth key derivation; challenge-signature login; short-lived JWT + rotating refresh
- **Storage:** IPFS content, IPNS metadata — the network is canonical; clients verify records cryptographically; CipherBox infra (Kubo, someguy) is accelerator-only and the API never serves records
- **Keys:** seeded per-scope derivation with key-regression epochs; rotation = O(1) root cut + lazy wave (`CONTEXT.md`)
- **One Rust core:** desktop links it natively, web loads it as WASM in a worker; one implementation, one KAT set
- **Sync:** pull-only focus-window polling, cache-first, offline op queue; no push in v2.0 (seam ready)
- **Desktop:** Tauri + FUSE mount (FUSE-T SMB on macOS, libfuse3 on Linux, WinFsp on Windows)
- **No TEE:** the republisher is a keyless re-PUT module inside the API; client-signed 90-day EOLs

## Out of Scope

- Billing/payments, mobile apps, real-time collaborative editing, team accounts
- Vault import (cut in v2), client-side search (deferred, designed-for)
- Executing anything against the frozen `v1` branch

## Verification with MCP Tools

### Puppeteer MCP Verification (REQUIRED)

**ALWAYS attempt to verify application changes using Puppeteer MCP** when it is available. This ensures implemented features work correctly at runtime.

**When to use Puppeteer MCP:**

- After implementing UI components
- After modifying styles or layouts
- After adding new pages or routes
- After any user-facing changes

**Verification workflow:** the dev server runs at `http://localhost:5173`. Navigate, screenshot, assert the elements and computed styles the change touches, then exercise the interaction. Element waits go through `puppeteer_evaluate` polling — there is no dedicated wait tool.

**If Puppeteer MCP is not available:**

- Document what needs human verification
- Provide manual test steps
- Flag items in VERIFICATION.md

### Pencil Design Files

Pencil design files exist at `designs/*.pen` (with `designs/DESIGN.md`) but are not actively maintained right now. `.pen` files are encrypted: read them only through the Pencil MCP tools — never `Read` or `grep` them directly.

## Git Workflow

### Branch Protection Rules

- **NEVER push directly to `main` branch** - all changes must go through feature branches and PRs
- Create feature branches with descriptive names (e.g., `feat/add-auth`, `fix/ipns-publish`)
- All commits should be made on feature branches first
- Merge to main only via pull requests

### Branch Naming

- `feat/` - New features
- `fix/` - Bug fixes
- `docs/` - Documentation updates
- `refactor/` - Code refactoring
- `chore/` - Maintenance tasks

### Commit Messages

Commits must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format:

```text
type(optional-scope): description

[optional body]
```

Valid types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Any scope string is allowed (e.g., `feat(api): add health endpoint`). A custom commitlint rule additionally rejects parenthesized text in the subject line (it breaks Release Please parsing).

Enforcement: commitlint is configured via `commitlint.config.js`, and PR titles are validated in CI by `.github/workflows/pr-title.yml`. Note that the husky `commit-msg` hook was replaced by an Entire CLI wrapper and currently does not run commitlint locally — follow the format regardless, since CI will reject non-conforming PR titles.

### No Tool Attribution

A commit message, a PR title, a PR body, an issue, and a review comment carry **no attribution to the tool that wrote them** — no `🤖 Generated with …` line, no `Co-Authored-By:` trailer naming an assistant, no session link. This holds however the text was produced.

The authorship that matters is the commit author and the PR author, which git and GitHub already record. A generated-by line adds nothing a reader can act on and turns every PR body into an advertisement.

Agent harnesses commonly append such a line by default. That default does not apply here: strip it before opening or editing a PR, and check the rendered body afterwards rather than trusting that it was never added.

### Mandatory PR Review Flow

Every code PR runs these review gates after it is opened as a **draft**, before it is driven toward merge — mandatory, not optional:

1. `/simplify` — tighten the diff: remove speculative generality, dead abstraction, and duplication.
2. `/security-review` — trust boundaries, fail-closed behavior, auth/expiry gates, injection, DoS/resource exhaustion, concurrency, and determinism seams.
3. `/crypto-privacy-review` — **required whenever the diff touches crypto**: `crates/core` primitives, key/seal material, or trust-boundary and fail-closed reads.

Run each on the PR's own diff (`git diff main...HEAD`) and fold real findings back into the code and tests before requesting a CodeRabbit/Greptile review. If a slash-command skill is unavailable in your environment, do a rigorous manual pass against that review's checklist instead — never skip a gate. Self-review is the floor, not the ceiling: layer an independent reviewer pass on crypto- and trust-critical PRs. A pure documentation change with no code surface is exempt.

{"body":"## Problem

Stage 3 of the adoption gate — the **one section, one signer** pin plus the walk over a `GrantSection`'s six seed-bearing structure kinds — lives in `crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs`. The gate's own module header promises the opposite:

> No crypto, no codec, and no cryptographic error code lives here: every cryptographic verdict is a core `CodecError` surfaced verbatim.

The layering is inverted, and the pin PR made it visible:

- **Core's bounds are now justified by an algorithm core cannot see.** `crates/core/src/seal/section.rs` (`MAX_HISTORY_LINKS`, `MAX_GRANT_BLOBS`) and `blueprint/core.md` both had to be rewritten to cite the engine's `pseudonyms + structures` work bound. Nothing in CI couples them; a change to the scan silently falsifies two core surfaces.
- **The verdict is core's.** `structure-signature-invalid` is a `TrustViolation::CHECKS` entry, so the engine emits a core trust verdict for a condition core does not define.
- **The stage-2 precondition is prose, not a type.** `authenticate_section_structures` is self-referential — it authenticates structures against the pseudonyms the section's *own* commitment names — so it is only a trust verdict once `verify_grant_set` has anchored that commitment. Today that is a doc comment guarding a `pub fn`.
- **`for_each_structure` had to be exported `#[doc(hidden)] pub`** so the engine KAT generator and suite could reach it, because the walk cannot live in core where both would naturally find it.

The premise that blocked this originally does not survive scrutiny: core already owns `GrantSetCommitment`, `Permission`, `verify_grant_set`, `GrantSection`, every `STRUCT_TAG_*`, and `verify_structure`. What it lacks is only the *composition* of things it already has.

## Fix

Move the predicate into `crates/core`, behind a witness type:

```rust
pub fn authenticate_section_structures(
    commitment: &VerifiedGrantSet,   // returned by verify_grant_set
    section: &GrantSection,
    scope: [u8; 16],
    epoch: u64,
) -> Result<(), CodecError>
```

`VerifiedGrantSet` turns the "run stage 2 first" doc block into an invariant the type system enforces. Then:

- the engine's stage 3 becomes the one-line composition the blueprint says it is, and `net/author.rs::check_scope_root` calls the same core function;
- `for_each_structure` and `committed_write_pseudonyms` stop needing `#[doc(hidden)] pub` on the engine;
- the mixed-signer reject vector moves into the core KAT manifest's `grant` family, where it can ride the existing `check_reject_family` harness instead of a bespoke engine set;
- `blueprint/core.md` and `seal/section.rs` get to state their own bound instead of cross-referencing engine.md.

## Counter-argument, recorded

Stage 3 is gate *policy*, not a primitive, and `blueprint/engine.md` currently places it in the engine's six-stage pipeline. Moving it drags "which entries are write-capable" into core. Weigh this before acting — the decision is a blueprint amendment either way, since engine.md's stage list and core.md's ownership boundary both move.

Surfaced by the `/simplify` altitude pass on the section-signer pin PR, which scoped it out deliberately: it touches `crates/core` primitives, `verify_grant_set`'s public signature, the core KAT manifest, and several engine call sites.

Part of the v2 build.

The witness type makes the stage-2 precondition an invariant the type system enforces; the mixed-signer reject vector moves into the core KAT grant family; blueprint/core.md and blueprint/engine.md each state their own bound, with engine.md's stage list pointing at the core predicate. The recorded counter-argument was weighed and declined: core already owns Permission and every other constituent, so the policy-vs-primitive line was already crossed by the data model.","createdAt":"2026-08-20T10:11:33Z"}],"createdAt":"2026-08-06T12:56:18Z","labels":["v2-build","comp:core"],"milestone":"post-cutover","number":1131,"state":"OPEN","title":"core: move the adoption gate's stage-3 section authentication into crates/core behind a verified-commitment witness","updatedAt":"2026-08-25T23:41:03Z"}

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

ever; the cut-epoch floor is what refuses the replay of one. A commitment
   that clears this stage whole raises that floor to its `cutEpoch`. The
   `/shared` classification path holds a record to this same stage and makes the
   same raise, so a device the owner cut — which adopts no post-cut record, and
   therefore never reaches the raise below — learns the cut too.
3. **Grant-section authentication** (scope roots) — every seed-bearing
   structure (grant blobs, owner blob, the optional owner-write-blob, ascent
   link, history links, write-body) verifies under **one** committed
   write-capable pseudonym via core's pure per-structure checks; any failure
   rejects the **whole record** as a trust violation (FSM1/cipher-box-next#39 D3). The
   owner-write-blob is optional on the wire, but a **present** one with a
   missing or invalid structure signature is a whole-record trust violation,
   never staleness (its signature is recomputed at the authenticated envelope
   epoch like every other structure, though its sealed AAD binds the write
   epoch).
4. **Sequence** — strictly newer than the durable per-name floor.
5. **Epoch** — epoch tag at or above the scope's durable epoch floor. An
   interior record below the floor is opened only by the three readers that the
   "sweep" section names.
6. **Unseal** — success required; core's trust-violation error class carries
   through fail-closed.

**One section, one signer** (stage 3). A section is a single rotator's work: it
re-seals and detached-signs every structure with its own writer pseudonym,
re-signing at the record's read epoch even the history links it carries forward
verbatim (`rotation/reseal.rs`). The gate therefore **pins** the pseudonym that
authenticated the section's first structure and requires every later structure
to verify under that key alone; a section signed by two committed pseudonyms is
unadoptable, not merely unusual.

It closes a **structure splice**: a structure lifted verbatim out of a different
record at the same scope and epoch, authored by a different committed writer,
recomputes an identical signed input — `scope`, `epoch`, `structTag`,
`recipientTag` and `H(ciphertext)` all match — so per-structure trial-verify
adopted it. It is also what bounds stage 3's work at `pseudonyms + structures`
rather than their product: without it an accepted contact commits 1024 write
pseudonyms of their own and spreads a section's signatures across them, buying
~1000x reader-CPU amplification for ~1284 signatures. The produce side runs the
same predicate release-active (`net/author.rs::check_scope_root`), so this build
never signs a section its own gate rejects.

lastPrompt: Is the following issue still valid? https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/1131  If its valid, this seems like something that should be implemented sooner rather than later as its a core change and…

content.text:
**Issue 1131 is still valid.** The stage-3 predicate lives in the engine today. Nothing in `crates/core` has a `VerifiedGrantSet` witness type. The owner decision from 2026-08-20 on the issue is recorded but not implemented. The issue sits in the `post-cutover` milestone under parent issue 989.

**What the code shows now**

- `authenticate_section_structures`, `for_each_structure`, and `committed_write_pseudonyms` are still `#[doc(hidden)] pub` in `crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:450-633`.
- The engine header at line 7 still promises "no crypto, no codec, and no cryptographic error code of its own". Stage 3 contradicts that promise.
- The engine KAT gate family with the mixed-signer reject vector still exists as a separate manifest at `crates/engine/kat/gate/manifest.json`. Issue 1132, which was blocked by 1131, is closed, but the family did not move.
- The blueprint still cross-references in both directions. `blueprint/core.md:328` justifies the core bounds with the engine's "pseudonyms + structures" bound. `blueprint/engine.md:212-229` owns the "one section, one signer" rule.

**The ripple grew after the issue was filed.** Two more engine consumers now read the same committed-writer set:

- `write_body_signer` in the gate, called from `net/rotation.rs` and stored on the cascade plane. It names the party for an abuse event.
- `is_committed_write_pseudonym`, called from `rotation/reseal.rs` on the produce side.

The witness type also changes the return type of `verify_grant_set_bound`. That function has five engine callers: the gate, `net/author.rs`, `rotation/rotate_write.rs`, `rotation/trigger.rs`, and `grants/received_status.rs` through the engine wrapper. Each caller must hold the witness and pass it to the predicate. The longer the wait, the more callers accrue.

**Size of the move**

| Layer | Files |
| --- | --- |
| core | `seal/grant.rs`, `seal/section.rs`, one new predicate module, `error.rs` unchanged, KAT manifest plus `examples/kat_gen.rs` |
| engine | `gate/adoption.rs`, `gate/mod.rs`, `net/author.rs`, `net/rotation.rs`, `rotation/reseal.rs`, `rotation/rotate_write.rs`, `rotation/trigger.rs`, `examples/kat_gen.rs`, `tests/kat_gate.rs`, `tests/adoption_gate.rs`, the engine gate KAT manifest |
| blueprint | `core.md` and `engine.md` |

The move changes no wire format and no KDF. It changes only which crate owns the composition, so the risk is a large diff, not a new trust surface.

**I agree it should land soon.** The reasons in the issue hold, and one is stronger now: the rotation and reseal paths grow new readers of the committed-writer set each wave, and each new reader is one more call site to rewire later.

**One gate before the code.** The move amends both blueprint documents, and the recorded rule is that a blueprint amendment goes through the ADR process in cipher-box-next first. No ADR exists for this decision yet. The owner comment on the issue is the full content of that ADR, so the ADR is a short one.

**Recommended path**

1. Move issue 1131 to the `v2.0.0` milestone.
2. Draft the ADR in cipher-box-next from the owner comment. Accept it.

# CipherBox - AI Agent Instructions

## Project Context

CipherBox is a privacy-first, zero-knowledge E2EE personal cloud storage system on IPFS/IPNS. The repo is mid-rewrite: **v2 is being built on `main`** against the blueprint corpus below; v1 is frozen on branch `v1` (tag `v1-freeze`) and receives no changes.

## Documentation Structure

The normative source of truth for the v2 build:

| Document                  | Purpose                                                       |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CONTEXT.md`              | The v2 ubiquitous language — use these terms, exactly         |
| `blueprint/core.md`       | `crates/core` — wire formats, crypto, KDF catalog, KAT regime |
| `blueprint/engine.md`     | `crates/engine` — the one stateful brain, seam traits, gates  |
| `blueprint/api.md`        | API residual surface, registry, mailbox, republisher          |
| `blueprint/web-client.md` | WASM hosting, tab leadership, `packages/client`, `apps/web`   |
| `blueprint/desktop.md`    | FS projection, host adapters, Tauri shell                     |
| `blueprint/testing.md`    | Suite map, CI gates, coverage policy                          |
| `blueprint/deploy.md`     | Freeze mechanics, release management, staging pipeline        |

The as-built v1 spec corpus, ADRs, and all design-decision history live in [FSM1/cipher-box-next](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next) (wayfinder map issue 1 indexes every decision). The `docs/` folder is v1 legacy — being rewritten during the build; trust `blueprint/` when they conflict.

## Terminology Standards

Use the v2 ubiquitous language defined in `CONTEXT.md` — every domain term (scope, epoch, ascent link, grant blob, adoption gate, floor law, eager set, …) has exactly one name there. General conventions: `publicKey`/`privateKey`/`ipnsName`/`ipnsRecord` spelled out in full camelCase for API fields, snake_case for database columns.

## Critical Security Rules

1. **Never** store `privateKey` or any seed in localStorage/sessionStorage
2. **Never** log sensitive keys or seeds
3. **Never** send unencrypted keys to the server — the server is zero-knowledge and NEVER sees plaintext or unencrypted keys
4. **All crypto lives in `crates/core`** — TypeScript has no codec or crypto of its own; never implement crypto in TS. **One exception: browser-held key custody via WebCrypto**, for a key that must be non-extractable, or must exist before the engine has a session. The engine cannot serve either case — a WASM implementation necessarily materializes key bytes in linear memory, which is the property non-extractability exists to deny, and before `start(secret)` there is no session to derive from. Conditions, all of them: the key protects local state only, it derives nothing in the KDF catalog, it touches no wire format and no KAT, and it never leaves WebCrypto. Two live instances — the Core Kit store's wrapping key (`apps/web/src/auth/sealedStore.ts`), and the device identity key that signs a device-approval exchange before reconstruction ([ADR 0009](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box-next/blob/main/decisions/0009-device-approval-is-a-bound-rendezvous.md)). Anything protocol-shaped is still Rust, without exception.
5. Primitives are fixed by `blueprint/core.md`: XChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing, BLAKE3 tree KDF, X25519 + HPKE key wrapping, REDACTED signing — no key derives outside the frozen KDF edge catalog
6. Every resolved record passes the adoption gate; a failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness
7. Clear sensitive material from memory after use (zeroize at the terminal owner only — a callee must not zero caller-owned buffers)
8. **Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry** — when a decode/verify path hard-rejects an invariant violation (a trust/malformed check), the matching encode/produce path MUST enforce the same invariant with a **release-active** check that returns `Err` — never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`, which are stripped in release. Otherwise a release build can sign and publish bytes its own decoder always rejects (an unopenable ledger/commitment/body). Keep these encode-side checks consistent with the `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` `assert_children_unique` convention, and cover them with a test that fires in a release build.

## API Contract and Clients

There are **no generated API clients** and no codegen loop. The engine contains the single hand-written Rust API client; the NestJS API's OpenAPI document is a committed docs artifact, not a build input. The contract is enforced by the live contract-test suite (the sdk-e2e descendant) running the real client against a real API instance on every PR — see `blueprint/testing.md`.

## Code Generation Guidelines

1. All engine, codec, and crypto logic is Rust (`crates/core`, `crates/engine`); TypeScript exists only in `packages/client` (WASM wrapper, browser seams), `packages/login` (host-agnostic login sequencing), `packages/auth-ui` (the React auth surfaces both hosts render), `apps/web` (React UI), `apps/desktop` (the Tauri shell chrome) and `tests/*` (the e2e harnesses)
2. Use `Uint8Array`/`Vec<u8>` for binary data, not strings
3. Determinism is injected: entropy, time, and policy enter as parameters/seam traits — never call clocks or RNGs directly in core/engine logic
4. A suite that asserts the behavior of a change and does not block a merge does not exist (`blueprint/testing.md` law 1, ADR 0050 D1): every suite is wired into a named CI gate the day it lands, and a measurement harness or a run against a deployed or long-horizon environment lives in the dispatch and scheduled tier with its code compiled in the PR gate; assert behavior, never source text

## Code Style

### Comments

Comments explain _why_, not _what_, and stay short. **If you need a paragraph-long comment to justify why a workaround is OK, the code is wrong — fix the code.** A long apologia for a hack is a smell: rework the code so it no longer needs defending, rather than documenting the shortcut. Reserve multi-line comments for genuinely non-obvious domain rationale — a spec citation, a cryptographic invariant, a wire-format or fail-closed constraint — not for excusing a shortcut.

Three recurring shapes of this smell go beyond excusing a hack — avoid all three:

- **Absence-justifying comments** — prose explaining why a path that is _not_ in the code does not happen (e.g. "`replay()` does not run here, so `decode_queue` is the only source at this stage"). It bloats the diff and rots into a falsehood the moment that path is wired — a stale in-code claim that actively misleads. Describe what the present code does; a bare cross-reference suffices if a reader must know a related path lives elsewhere.
- **Unchanged-code apologia** — a doc block defending code this change does not modify (e.g. why a parameter stays a raw borrow, on a function the diff leaves untouched). It is scope creep into untouched code and reads as pre-emptive defensiveness. Leave that rationale where it already lives.
- **Tracker references** — a bare `#1234` claims something about the _tracker_, not the code, so nothing in CI, review, or the type system catches it drifting when the issue closes, splits, or gets re-scoped. State the condition instead: `the real wiring is #1026` becomes `the real wiring is not landed`, which is checkable from the code and stops being true in the same diff that falsifies it. Enforced by `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` (the **Tracker Refs** gate). Exempt: citations of the frozen decision corpus, whether written `FSM1/cipher-box-next#32` or bare as `#33 D6` — this repo's issue numbers share an ever-increasing counter with its PRs and passed 1000 long ago, so a one- or two-digit `#NN` can only be cipher-box-next. Commit messages and PR bodies are also exempt: they are timestamped and do not rot.

State genuine non-obvious domain rationale **once**, at its home (the type or definition), not restated on every caller. These cost real review cycles — `/simplify`, CodeRabbit, and Greptile all flag them.

Length discipline for the permitted domain-rationale exception: state each invariant **once** and prefer a one-line cross-reference to the blueprint / `CONTEXT.md` over re-deriving it in prose. Do not narrate the happy path — the code is the narrative, and a comment restating what the next lines plainly do rots out of sync and misleads. A module header past ~25 lines is almost always restating the spec: keep only the rationale that is non-obvious _from the code itself_ and cite the blueprint for the rest.

## Architecture Pillars

- **Auth:** Web3Auth key derivation; challenge-signature login; short-lived JWT + rotating refresh
- **Storage:** IPFS content, IPNS metadata — the network is canonical; clients verify records cryptographically; CipherBox infra (Kubo, someguy) is accelerator-only and the API never serves records
- **Keys:** seeded per-scope derivation with key-regression epochs; rotation = O(1) root cut + lazy wave (`CONTEXT.md`)
- **One Rust core:** desktop links it natively, web loads it as WASM in a worker; one implementation, one KAT set
- **Sync:** pull-only focus-window polling, cache-first, offline op queue; no push in v2.0 (seam ready)
- **Desktop:** Tauri + FUSE mount (FUSE-T SMB on macOS, libfuse3 on Linux, WinFsp on Windows)
- **No TEE:** the republisher is a keyless re-PUT module inside the API; client-signed 90-day EOLs

## Out of Scope

- Billing/payments, mobile apps, real-time collaborative editing, team accounts
- Vault import (cut in v2), client-side search (deferred, designed-for)
- Executing anything against the frozen `v1` branch

## Verification with MCP Tools

### Puppeteer MCP Verification (REQUIRED)

**ALWAYS attempt to verify application changes using Puppeteer MCP** when it is available. This ensures implemented features work correctly at runtime.

**When to use Puppeteer MCP:**

- After implementing UI components
- After modifying styles or layouts
- After adding new pages or routes
- After any user-facing changes

**Verification workflow:** the dev server runs at `http://localhost:5173`. Navigate, screenshot, assert the elements and computed styles the change touches, then exercise the interaction. Element waits go through `puppeteer_evaluate` polling — there is no dedicated wait tool.

**If Puppeteer MCP is not available:**

- Document what needs human verification
- Provide manual test steps
- Flag items in VERIFICATION.md

### Pencil Design Files

Pencil design files exist at `designs/*.pen` (with `designs/DESIGN.md`) but are not actively maintained right now. `.pen` files are encrypted: read them only through the Pencil MCP tools — never `Read` or `grep` them directly.

## Git Workflow

### Branch Protection Rules

- **NEVER push directly to `main` branch** - all changes must go through feature branches and PRs
- Create feature branches with descriptive names (e.g., `feat/add-auth`, `fix/ipns-publish`)
- All commits should be made on feature branches first
- Merge to main only via pull requests

### Branch Naming

- `feat/` - New features
- `fix/` - Bug fixes
- `docs/` - Documentation updates
- `refactor/` - Code refactoring
- `chore/` - Maintenance tasks

### Commit Messages

Commits must follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format:

```text
type(optional-scope): description

[optional body]
```

Valid types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `perf`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `revert`. Any scope string is allowed (e.g., `feat(api): add health endpoint`). A custom commitlint rule additionally rejects parenthesized text in the subject line (it breaks Release Please parsing).

Enforcement: commitlint is configured via `commitlint.config.js`, and PR titles are validated in CI by `.github/workflows/pr-title.yml`. Note that the husky `commit-msg` hook was replaced by an Entire CLI wrapper and currently does not run commitlint locally — follow the format regardless, since CI will reject non-conforming PR titles.

### No Tool Attribution

A commit message, a PR title, a PR body, an issue, and a review comment carry **no attribution to the tool that wrote them** — no `🤖 Generated with …` line, no `Co-Authored-By:` trailer naming an assistant, no session link. This holds however the text was produced.

The authorship that matters is the commit author and the PR author, which git and GitHub already record. A generated-by line adds nothing a reader can act on and turns every PR body into an advertisement.

Agent harnesses commonly append such a line by default. That default does not apply here: strip it before opening or editing a PR, and check the rendered body afterwards rather than trusting that it was never added.

### Mandatory PR Review Flow

Every code PR runs these review gates after it is opened as a **draft**, before it is driven toward merge — mandatory, not optional:

1. `/simplify` — tighten the diff: remove speculative generality, dead abstraction, and duplication.
2. `/security-review` — trust boundaries, fail-closed behavior, auth/expiry gates, injection, DoS/resource exhaustion, concurrency, and determinism seams.
3. `/crypto-privacy-review` — **required whenever the diff touches crypto**: `crates/core` primitives, key/seal material, or trust-boundary and fail-closed reads.

Run each on the PR's own diff (`git diff main...HEAD`) and fold real findings back into the code and tests before requesting a CodeRabbit/Greptile review. If a slash-command skill is unavailable in your environment, do a rigorous manual pass against that review's checklist instead — never skip a gate. Self-review is the floor, not the ceiling: layer an independent reviewer pass on crypto- and trust-critical PRs. A pure documentation change with no code surface is exempt.

### Releases & Versioning

See the `releases` skill (`.claude/skills/releases/SKILL.md`) for the v2 release scheme, version surfaces, staging tag pipeline, and the v1 freeze. Normative source: `blueprint/deploy.md`.
